stimulus.content: Vertical farms grow crops in stacked trays under controlled light. Because the growing area is multiplied by the number of layers, a warehouse can produce what several hectares of field would yield, using about five per cent of the water. The cost sits in the electricity: lighting and climate control account for roughly half of operating expenses. Where power is cheap and land is scarce, the arithmetic works. Where the opposite holds, it does not.

stem: According to the passage, roughly how much of a vertical farm's operating expenses go to lighting and climate control?

choices.text: half
a quarter
one hectare's worth
five per cent
all of them

explanation:
The third sentence states it directly: lighting and climate control account for roughly half of operating expenses.

The figure of five per cent in the passage refers to water use, not to electricity.

distractorRationale.B: No such figure appears in the passage.
distractorRationale.C: Confuses a unit of area with a share of cost.
distractorRationale.D: Refers to water use, not to the cost of power.
distractorRationale.E: The passage says roughly half, not all.

stem: According to the passage, how does a vertical farm multiply its growing area?

choices.text: by lowering the cost of electricity
by stacking trays in layers
by using less water
by extending the growing season

explanation:

Water saving is a separate benefit, not the mechanism that multiplies area.

distractorRationale.A: The passage says electricity is the main cost, not a way to gain area.
distractorRationale.C: A benefit of the method, not the way area is multiplied.
distractorRationale.E: The point of the method is that no field is used.

stem: What is the main point of the last two sentences of the passage?

choices.text: Vertical farming is always cheaper than field farming
Electricity prices are falling worldwide
Whether vertical farming makes economic sense depends on local conditions
Vertical farming should replace field farming everywhere
Land scarcity is the only factor that matters

explanation:
The two sentences set the same calculation against opposite conditions: cheap power with scarce land makes it work, and the reverse makes it fail.

The point is therefore conditional — the method is neither universally viable nor universally unviable.

distractorRationale.A: The passage says the opposite in the final sentence.
distractorRationale.B: No trend in electricity prices is given.
distractorRationale.D: No recommendation of that kind is made.
distractorRationale.E: Power cost is named alongside land scarcity.

stem: Which additional information would be most useful in judging whether a vertical farm should be built in a particular city?

choices.text: the number of vegetables sold in that city last year
the colour of the lights used in the trays
the average height of warehouses in that city
the local price of electricity and of land
the water content of the crops grown

explanation: The passage identifies exactly two conditions that decide the arithmetic: the cost of power and the scarcity of land. Knowing both for a particular city applies the passage's own test.

distractorRationale.A: Sales volume speaks to demand, not to the cost condition the passage sets out.
distractorRationale.B: A technical detail the passage never links to viability.
distractorRationale.C: Building height affects layout but not the decisive costs named.
distractorRationale.E: Water use is already stated as low in every case.

stimulus.content: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is often pictured as a floating island of bottles and bags. Sampling tells a different story. Most of the material is smaller than a grain of rice, spread thinly through the upper water column across an area larger than many countries. That is why clean-up is difficult: a net fine enough to catch the fragments also catches the plankton that feed the ocean.

stem: According to the passage, most of the material in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is ...

choices.text: made of glass
bottles and bags
found on the sea floor
larger than a plankton net
smaller than a grain of rice

explanation:
The third sentence states it: most of the material is smaller than a grain of rice, spread thinly through the upper water column.

Bottles and bags belong to the common picture that the passage sets out to correct.

distractorRationale.A: Material type beyond that is not specified.
distractorRationale.B: Named as the popular image, which sampling contradicts.
distractorRationale.C: The passage places the material in the upper water column.
distractorRationale.D: The passage says fragments are small enough that fine nets are needed.

stem: Why does the passage say clean-up is difficult?

choices.text: A net fine enough to catch the fragments would also catch plankton
The patch lies too far from any coastline
The material sinks faster than it can be collected
The fragments dissolve when touched
No country has claimed responsibility for the area

explanation:
The final sentence gives the reason directly: because the pieces are so small, any net fine enough to catch them also catches the plankton that feed the ocean.

The difficulty is therefore not distance or ownership but the size of the fragments.

distractorRationale.C: The passage places the material in the upper water column, not sinking.

stem: What is the writer's main purpose in the second sentence, «Sampling tells a different story»?

to argue that sampling methods are unreliable
to explain how samples are collected
to compare two different patches of debris

distractorRationale.A: No researchers are praised or even named.
distractorRationale.C: The passage relies on sampling rather than doubting it.
distractorRationale.D: The method of sampling is never described.

stem: Which statement is best supported by the passage?

choices.text: Clean-up efforts have already succeeded

explanation:

The passage says nothing about the patch's size relative to belief, its growth, or the success of any effort.

distractorRationale.A: The passage describes clean-up as difficult, not accomplished.
distractorRationale.B: Bottles are named as part of the mistaken picture.
distractorRationale.E: The passage says it spreads across an area larger than many countries.

stem: Which situation would most weaken the case for vertical farming as the passage presents it?

choices.text: a country facing a shortage of fresh water
a city with expensive land and cheap hydroelectric power
a city where warehouses stand empty
a place where vegetables must be imported by air
a region with abundant farmland and high electricity prices

explanation: The passage makes the case depend on two conditions: cheap power and scarce land. A region with plenty of farmland and expensive electricity fails both at once, which is precisely the case the final sentence describes.

distractorRationale.A: Water scarcity favours the method, given the five per cent figure.
distractorRationale.B: Satisfies both conditions and therefore strengthens the case.
distractorRationale.C: Empty warehouses lower the cost of space.
distractorRationale.D: Costly imports strengthen the argument for local production.

stem: Which sentence best summarises the passage about the garbage patch?

choices.text: The patch consists mainly of tiny fragments spread thinly, which makes removing it hard without harming marine life.

Fine nets are the most promising technology for cleaning the ocean.

stimulus.content: When Amara returned to the house after eleven years, the mango tree in the yard had outgrown the roof. She had planted it the week before she left, a stick no taller than her knee, and had not thought of it once. Now it dropped fruit onto the tin with a sound like knocking. She stood at the gate a long while, unwilling to admit that something had been getting on with its life in her absence.

stem: How long had Amara been away from the house?

choices.text: since childhood
a single season
eleven years
the passage does not say
one week

explanation:
The opening sentence states it directly: she returned after eleven years.

The week mentioned later is when she planted the tree, just before leaving.

distractorRationale.A: Her age when leaving is not stated.
distractorRationale.D: The figure is given in the first sentence.
distractorRationale.E: Refers to when the tree was planted, not to her absence.

stem: What does the detail that Amara «had not thought of it once» most suggest?

choices.text: She disliked the tree when she planted it
She expected the tree to die
She planted the tree for someone else
She had left the place entirely behind her

explanation: The detail is placed between planting the tree and finding it grown. Not thinking of it once in eleven years shows how completely she had put the place out of mind — which is why its growth surprises her.

distractorRationale.B: Expectation of death is never indicated.
distractorRationale.C: The passage says she planted it herself, with no mention of another person.
distractorRationale.E: The passage describes a single return after eleven years.

stem: What does the comparison «a sound like knocking» contribute to the passage?

choices.text: It explains why the tree grew so tall
It shows that the fruit is unripe
It indicates that someone is at the gate
It suggests the roof is about to collapse
It suggests the house is calling her back, as a visitor knocks at a door

explanation: Knocking is what a visitor does at a door, and Amara is standing at the gate, unwilling to come in. The comparison turns the falling fruit into a summons, which is why the image is placed just before her hesitation.

distractorRationale.A: The sound has no bearing on the tree's growth.
distractorRationale.B: Ripeness is not at issue; the fruit is falling.
distractorRationale.C: The only person present is Amara herself.
